transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Start: 15:30 PT
Duration: 48 minutes
Recordings: enabled

Summary (auto): quick run on cost per token, batching and caching levers, committed vs pay-as-you-go, pilot next steps

[00:00] Lena Park: hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. i'm lena from redwood, account exec. quick intros?
[00:06] Evelyn Cho: hi lena, evelyn, head of ml at crimson analytics. we run a bunch of quant models and are exploring LLM augmentation across research and product.
[00:13] Samir Patel: samir, vp engineering. i'm mainly worried about infra and budgets.
[00:17] Ravi Nair: ravi, quant researcher, will own some evaluation and sampling for us.
[00:21] Marco Diaz: marco here, solutions engineer on redwood, i’ll dive into perf/cost tradeoffs.
[00:25] Jules Martin: jules, infra, will be reviewing networking and kms stuff.
[00:28] Lena Park: great. objective for today: understand your volume, latency targets, and what pricing model makes sense - hosted api vs dedicated pool vs private. also we can talk batching, kv/prefix caching, and quantization levers.

[02:05] Evelyn Cho: high level - we expect about 400M tokens a month across a mix of chat/assistant prompts and some embeddings. our initial budget target is around 15k to 25k a month, but we can be flexible if unit economics make sense.
[02:24] Lena Park: ok that gives us a baseline. 400M tokens is helpful. do you have split prompt vs completion tokens or avg response length?
[02:33] Ravi Nair: average response is 120 tokens, prompt ~40 tokens. maybe 60% generation, 40% embeddings.

[04:10] Marco Diaz: quick framing: hosted pricing is pay-as-you-go per token; dedicated is a committed monthly pool - lower per-token cost because of reserved GPUs; private is a customer-managed deployment often with a platform fee plus infra. for cost levers: batching increases throughput and lowers per-token cost but can add tail latency; prefix/KV caching reduces total tokens sent to model for repeated queries, sometimes 20-60% token savings depending on repetition; and quantization (4-bit/8-bit) lowers GPU memory and can reduce instance cost.

[05:02] Samir Patel: what's the ballpark hosted per-token? and dedicated committed numbers? we just need an apples-to-apples comparison.
[05:12] Lena Park: rough examples - hosted might be in the $0.0005-0.0010 per input+output token range for higher-capacity models (this is illustrative), dedicated can push effective marginal cost down significantly depending on commitment - think 30-60% lower per-token if you fully utilize the pool. private has bigger fixed costs but gives you predictable unit cost once infra is amortized.

[06:01] Evelyn Cho: ok. our target is around $0.0003-0.0005 effective per token otherwise the ROI doesn't work for a lot of our products. is that realistic?
[06:14] Marco Diaz: at 400M tokens, dedicated becomes attractive. example: if you commit to a monthly pool and use batching and KV caching aggressively, we can show models in the $0.00025-0.00045 range in our internal examples - depends on model choice and caching hit-rate.

[07:30] Ravi Nair: can you explain how caching is measured? we have a lot of repeated prefixes in finance queries.
[07:37] Marco Diaz: sure. prefix or KV cache stores the transformer key/value cache for previously seen prefixes so you don't re-send or re-compute tokens. hit-rate is based on how often queries share prefixes. in trading workflows with templated prompts, we often see 30-50% reduction in generated tokens; in more dynamic chat it can be lower. for your use-case with templated research queries, i’d expect higher hit-rate.

[09:20] Samir Patel: what about latency tradeoffs with batching? our product needs p95 < 250ms for some flows.
[09:28] Marco Diaz: batching increases throughput by grouping requests; we can configure batching windows. smaller windows preserve latency but reduce batching efficiency. we typically recommend hybrid: latency-sensitive paths on a low-latency pool (smaller batch sizes, reserved capacity) and background requests on high-batch pools. dedicated lets you carve out low-latency lanes.

[11:02] Evelyn Cho: any numbers - like what's p95 impact if we go heavy on batching?
[11:07] Marco Diaz: a rough rule: moving from single-request execution to 32-request batch can increase average latency slightly but improve tokens/sec massively. p95 for batched pools depends on target window; in our benchmarks, well-configured batching for throughput-first endpoints still kept p95 around 500-700ms, but low-latency lanes we keep under 200-300ms. again model size matters.

[13:00] Samir Patel: so we need to map endpoints by SLO. p95 < 250 for interactive widgets, background summarization can be higher.

[13:30] Lena Park: exactly. we typically do a cost allocation model: map each route to expected qps, SLO, and token sizes, then model per-token and infra cost. we can send you our cost model spreadsheet.

[15:05] Ravi Nair: quantization - how safe is 4-bit for accuracy on retrieval-augmented tasks? we can't degrade output quality much.
[15:13] Marco Diaz: quantization varies by model; 8-bit is usually safe for most tasks, 4-bit can cause small drops depending on model and task. for retrieval-augmented generation we recommend running evaluation sets; sometimes 4-bit is fine for embeddings+rerank but for generation-sensitive scoring you may prefer 8-bit or fp16. we can include quality regressions in the pilot.

[17:40] Evelyn Cho: security questions: SSO, SAML, audit logs, KMS/HSM, data residency. can hosted meet our compliance needs?
[17:50] Lena Park: hosted supports SSO/SAML, RBAC, audit logs; we integrate with KMS for key management. for stricter needs we recommend private with customer-managed KMS or Dedicated with VPC peering and stricter data retention policies. we will share SOC2 and security docs.

[19:05] Jules Martin: for private deployments do you support on-prem or only VPC?
[19:10] Marco Diaz: both - VPC deployments and an on-prem package for air-gapped scenarios. on-prem is a larger engagement and has different licensing.

[21:00] Samir Patel: ok, back to numbers. if we commit to a dedicated pool, what's the commitment level to hit our price target?
[21:12] Lena Park: quick example: to get to ~$0.00035 effective token cost at 400M tokens, you’d likely need a mid-size reserved pool - for example a monthly commit in the mid five digits (roughly $20k-30k) depending on model selection and utilization. exact pricing depends on contract term and expected burst patterns.

[23:05] Evelyn Cho: that's in our range. can you show a concrete example in the pricing sheet? we need hosted comparatives too because we may start hosted and move to dedicated.
[23:13] Lena Park: yes, we'll produce a hosted vs dedicated vs private apples-to-apples that includes assumptions: token split, batching gains, cache hit-rate, and quantization.

[25:00] Marco Diaz: for benchmarking, we usually run a 3-day pilot with your prompt set: measure p50/p95 latency, throughput, and token consumption; we simulate expected qps and run with batching and caching enabled. sample size: 1-5M tokens is typical for initial signal; we can scale up if you want tighter confidence.

[26:22] Ravi Nair: we can provide 1M tokens of representative prompts initially.

[26:35] Marco Diaz: perfect. we'll instrument with tracing so you see token counts by route and caching stats.

[28:00] Evelyn Cho: what about overage and burst behavior? month with spiky usage.

[28:06] Lena Park: dedicated contracts include burst options; you can have baseline reserved capacity and burst on hosted or a higher capacity tier. routing policies can failover to hosted if dedicated is saturated.

[30:10] Samir Patel: SLA questions - uptime and latency SLOs for dedicated?

[30:16] Lena Park: dedicated has SLA-backed uptime and latency targets, with monitoring in the console. we'll include SLA language in the contract.

[31:50] Jules Martin: integration complexity - how much work for our infra team?

[31:56] Marco Diaz: typical integration is an API key and VPC peering for dedicated/private. for private on-prem there's more work (deployment manifests, network, KMS). we provide a runbook and support. estimated 2-4 weeks for dedicated integration for a small team.

[34:10] Evelyn Cho: can you send examples of customers in finance to reference their unit econ stories?

[34:16] Lena Park: yes we'll anonymize but can share examples and benchmark anonymized numbers.

[35:50] Ravi Nair: question on embeddings cost - are they charged same per token? they often bill per embed unit; curious how you model that.

[35:58] Marco Diaz: embeddings are typically priced differently (per-embedding-unit or per-token depending on provider). in our model we convert embeddings to equivalent token cost to make apples-to-apples, and we'll show that breakout in the spreadsheet.

[38:00] Samir Patel: curious about monitoring and cost allocation by route.

[38:06] Priya Rao: our console provides per-route token breakdown, cost by token and latency, and trace links so you can attribute spend back to product features.

[40:20] Evelyn Cho: ok recap - you're going to send pricing, sample econ model, security docs, and benchmark plan. we provide prompts and estimate.

[40:32] Lena Park: yes. next step: we'll email pricing sheet and schedule pilot. Marco, you'll own the bench test setup.

[41:05] Marco Diaz: i'll share the benchmark harness and default config. propose pilot week Mar 16, 3 days, 1M tokens baseline.

[41:20] Jules Martin: that works for infra. i'll confirm KMS details.

[42:40] Ravi Nair: one more thing - can we test 4-bit vs 8-bit quality delta as part of pilot?

[42:47] Marco Diaz: yes, we'll add a quantization arm to the pilot and produce quality regression metrics on your eval set.

[44:00] Lena Park: excellent. i'll send follow-up with action items and calendar invite for the pilot planning.

[44:30] Evelyn Cho: thanks, good call.
[44:33] Samir Patel: thanks everyone.
[44:35] Lena Park: thanks all. end recording.
